title: The NLstart2run study: Training-related factors associated with running-related injuries in novice runners
authors: Kluitenberg B, van der Worp H, Huisstede BM, Hartgens F, Diercks R, Verhagen E, van Middelkoop M
journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
population: Novice runners in a 6-week Start to Run programme (Netherlands)
findings: 1696 novices completed weekly diaries of running exposure and injury during a 6-week novice programme; volume (min), frequency and mean RPE over the seven days before each training session were analysed as time-varying exposures in an extended Cox regression.
Running at a higher intensity (RPE) in the previous week was associated with a higher injury risk.
Running frequency was not significantly associated with injury, but there was a trend toward running three times per week being more hazardous than two.

Lower running volume was associated with a higher injury risk; the authors read this as running more than 60 min at a lower intensity being least injurious, but call the finding contrary to expectation and presumably due to other factors, and say it should not be used plainly as a guideline for novices.
limitations: Observational with time-varying confounding (people who are already hurting run less, which would produce the volume finding); the frequency effect is a non-significant trend; the programme was 6 weeks only; no run-walk versus continuous contrast.
implications: Keep intensity easy in the first weeks: the only clear adverse signal was higher RPE the week before.
Do not use this paper to justify a higher floor volume or to cut frequency to 2 days; the volume and frequency signals are weak and probably confounded.
Supports a conservative evidence grade (C/D) for any start-dose parameter that rests on frequency.
